title: Bourbon Street jazz revivals and the jitney dance halls
summary: Bandstand on Bourbon Street, crowds, jazz returning every 25 years and its roots in taxi dance halls.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Louis Escobeda played trumpet and vibra harp. Ah. That was when the bandstand faced the front of Bourbon Street. You know what I'm saying? Faced Bourbon Street. We saw it completely renovated three times, enlarged on account of it. And eyeballs at that time started off at 65 cents. And many of the time I had a standing line outside waiting to get in to hear that jazz that we played because it was another renovation, you see? Jazz that almost became awake again, almost like a circle on a wheel, like a spoke on a wheel every 25 years. It looked to me like it was that way.
You mean the people got interested in it?
The trend for jazz until now, today jazz is almost seem, you would say, permanent.

Because during the time that I first came on Bourbon Street there were no jazz bands at all. They didn't play jazz. The only place that you ever heard jazz was in the Jitney dance halls. And that's where all of these fine jazz musicians from New Orleans started was in these taxi dance halls. The fine, the Vita. Such places as that.
So they had music in the quarter, but what kind of music was it?

It was cabaret style. Regular dance music of popular music at the time. The music that was popular at that time. For instance, Yes Sir, That's My Baby. Margie. All of those things. But the things that were already written were some 25 or 30 years the generation before that. stuff very shady, Mahogany Hall was. It's hard for me to go back further than that for the simple reason I am not a native of New Orleans. Had I been a native of New Orleans, I could tell you how it all began, so to speak. But I'm not. I'm a native of Mississippi. And all of those things that I learned, and all of those tunes such as the Clarinet Marmalade and the Jasmine Blues, I learned from the band that my brother was playing in. Don't you see? Because when they'd come to Gulfport or Biloxi to play, they used to bring me over there and I'd sit on the floor in the wings barefooted. Ten-year-old kid listening to that and just absolutely. And from the time that I was four and five years old, my mother used to let me go to the dances that they had all night long. When W.C. Handy played up in the courthouse, the courthouse whole top floor, the courthouse was cleared and they had dancing all night long. They had two bands. And that happened only once or twice a year. But my mother, knowing how much I loved that, used to let me go. Because my older brothers were there dancing, don't you see? And there was no such animal as being in danger in those days.
